transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-21
Start time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Noah Rivera (Redwood Solutions Eng), Priya Shah (Redwood SRE); Evelyn Park (Arcturus Head of ML Ops), Samir Gupta (Arcturus Infra Lead), Laura Kim (Arcturus Security), Tom Vasquez (Data Eng), Rita Moreno (Product)

Auto-generated summary (may be noisy):
The team ran through load synthesis methodology for apples-to-apples comparisons. Focus on KV-cache warmup, sequence length distribution, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem networking. Agreed next steps: share runbook, run microbenchmarks, schedule on-prem smoke test. Security asked for SOC2 and KMS notes.

Topics: load synthesis, kv cache profiling, batching windows, quantization profile selection, VPC peering, SLO alignment, sample prompts, artifact links

References: runbook draft (link: https://redwood.s3/runbooks/load-synth-v1.xlsx), sample k6 script (link: https://gist.github.com/redwood/load-synth-k6), prompt set (placeholder link sent after call)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Quick roll call then we'll jump into the runbook and the microbench plan. Jordan, do you want to intro the goals?
[00:15] Jordan Li: Sure, thanks Maya. Hi all, Jordan from Redwood SE. The goal today is to align on a repeatable load-synthesis and KV-cache profiling approach so Arcturus can compare hosted vs dedicated vs on-prem results in an apples-to-apples way. We'll cover prompt sets, warmup, steady-state window, concurrency models, and the measurement artifacts we collect.
[00:37] Evelyn Park: Perfect. For context, our primary production use case is real-time summarization for inbound customer transcripts. We have bursty load with hour-long spikes, SLO is 200ms p95 for short summaries and 800ms p95 for long-form. Cost is a big factor, too.
[00:52] Samir Gupta: Also important: we have strict egress and audit requirements, which push us toward VPC/private deployment. We'll want to see on-prem numbers because some hosts are not allowed to leave our network.
[01:05] Laura Kim: Security will want to validate KMS integration and audit logs. We'll need proof of encrypted at-rest keys and access logs.
[01:12] Jordan Li: Absolutely — we'll include KMS noise in the runbook and capture end-to-end timing with and without KMS operations to show overhead.

[01:30] Noah Rivera: Quick note on naming: when I say 'KV-cache' today I'm referring to the model's key-value attention cache/kv-store — the prefix cache that reduces repeated token work. Sometimes telemetry calls it "K V cache" or "kv cack" in transcriptions, so apologies in advance for the typos.
[01:45] Rita Moreno: Thanks. On prompts, we can provide 3 canonical prompt templates: short summary (~50 tokens), medium (~200 tokens), long (~1k tokens). We can also add few edge-case prompts that cause very long contexts.

[02:05] Jordan Li: Great. Proposed benchmark phases:
- Phase 0: Baseline cold-first-token latency (no cache, min batch size)
- Phase 1: Warmup and steady-state (KV cache warmed with representative prefixes)
- Phase 2: Burst test (spike concurrency, autoscale behavior)
- Phase 3: Quantization sweep (FP16/INT8/QLoRA profiles)
- Phase 4: Network topology variants (hosted vs VPC vs on-prem)

[02:35] Samir Gupta: For our legal auditors, we need to see identical prompt sets used across every run and the seed for any randomness. Are you planning deterministic seeds for sampling?
[02:45] Jordan Li: Yes, set seed for sampling and log RNG state. For temperature-style runs we recommend documenting the seed and using greedy/test sampling profiles as separate runs.

[03:10] Tom Vasquez: How do you suggest we warm the KV-cache? Our traffic is not prefix-heavy, so warming might be tricky.
[03:19] Jordan Li: Two-pronged approach: synthetic prefix replay plus shadow-run traces. Synthetic replay uses the prompt set to prefill prefixes across model shards; shadow runs replay a window from your production logs with privacy-preserving anonymization. We'll provide scripts for both.
[03:37] Maya Chen: We'll also capture cache hit-rate time series. Important to capture not just aggregate QPS but per-shard cache hit ratio, and the performance delta when hit vs miss.

[04:00] [short crosstalk] Evelyn Park: ...so if the hit rate is only 30% in production we'll see very different latencies than your ideal case.
[04:10] Jordan Li: Exactly. That's why the runbook insists on reporting both cold and warm percentiles and overlaying them with hit rates.

[05:00] Priya Shah: On batching: we recommend continuous-batching windows of 10–30ms for latency-sensitive workloads. But that only works if your arrival distribution supports slight queueing. For strict 200ms p95 we typically set a 10ms batching window and a max batch size tuned by profiling.
[05:25] Samir Gupta: If we set 10ms window, that's more CPU/GPU utilization but might add tail latency during spikes. How do you recommend trading off?
[05:35] Jordan Li: The runbook includes a tradeoff matrix: smaller windows = better p95 for single-request service; larger windows increase throughput and amortize kernel overhead. For spikes we suggest autoscaling policies with fast scale-up and a fallback to a slightly cheaper model variant to avoid SLO misses. We'll include config snippets.

[06:05] Rita Moreno: On quantization: our models are currently FP16 on-prem. We are curious about INT8/4-bit profiles to cut cost. What do you recommend for apples-to-apples quality checks?
[06:15] Noah Rivera: Keep a fixed eval prompt set and run the exact prompts across quantization profiles. Use metric diffs (ROUGE/BLEU for summarization, plus a small human eval sample). We recommend tracking perplexity and a few domain-specific pass/fail checks. Also capture latency & memory footprint for each profile.

[06:45] Laura Kim: Security question: if you use shared hosting, how do you separate telemetry and logs? Can we get tenant-level audit logs and SSO integration?
[06:53] Maya Chen: Yes — hosted provides tenant-scoped audit logs and SSO/SAML integration. But we'll include a section in the runbook comparing the log availability and retention windows between hosted and private deployments.

[07:20] Jordan Li: Now I'll walk through the sample k6 load generator. (Jordan shares screen) The script uses a mixture of open and closed loop patterns. We recommend closed-loop for latency measurement and open-loop for stress throughput.
[07:40] [00:08:00] Jordan Li: Example schedule in the runbook: 15m ramp-up, 1h steady-state (collect heatmap), 30m burst with 3x concurrency, 15m cooldown. Collect per-request telemetry with timestamps and optionally push traces to jaeger.
[08:05] Tom Vasquez: What telemetry fields should we capture?
[08:12] Jordan Li: At minimum: request_id, timestamp, model_variant, sequence_length_in, sequence_length_out, tokens_generated, kv_cache_hit (bool), batch_size, host_shard_id, p95/p99 latency, cpu/gpu utilization snapshot. We also suggest a small header with seed and quantization profile.

[08:45] Evelyn Park: For apples-to-apples, how do we control for hardware differences? We'll probably test our on-prem A100s vs Redwood Dedicated gpus which might be different.
[08:55] Noah Rivera: We'll normalize by throughput per GPU or cost per 1k tokens as a post-processing metric. Also include kernel-level counters and batch-efficiency metrics. The runbook has a normalization spreadsheet template so you can compare tokens/sec per GPU and dollars-per-million-tokens.

[09:30] Laura Kim: On VPC peering and network — our security team requires diagram and egress controls. Samir, can you briefly highlight the network constraints?
[09:38] Samir Gupta: We have strict egress rules. Anything leaving the VPC requires inspection and must go through our proxy. A full on-prem install might be easier but needs operational support. We want to know what the Redwood private package requires in terms of nodes, ports, and KMS endpoints.
[09:55] Priya Shah: For private on-prem, we provide a control plane shim that can run in your VPC and a local serving plane. The runbook includes a checklist: required ports (gRPC endpoints), recommended NIC MTU, and expected bandwidth for model weights. KMS calls are optional to measure.

[10:25] Jordan Li: Let's talk about result artifacts and naming conventions. Use stable filenames like arcturus_20260821_phase1_cold.csv, include a small JSON sidecar with run metadata to avoid confusion.
[10:38] Rita Moreno: We'll need those CSVs to feed into our internal SRE dashboards. Is there a template?
[10:42] Jordan Li: Yes the runbook includes a mapping to Grafana/Prometheus metric names and a sample ingest pipeline. We'll send the link after the call.

[11:05] [short break; background noise]
[11:30] [00:38:00] Jordan Li: Back to quantization — we encountered in prior customers a surprising effect where INT8 reduced GPU latency but increased CPU-side packing time. So include host CPU snapshots.
[11:47] Samir Gupta: Good point. We monitor both sides.

[12:05] Tom Vasquez: How do you validate quality regressions automatically? We can't afford manual A/B for all runs.
[12:13] Noah Rivera: Use an evaluation harness: embed a small human-in-the-loop sample set of 100 items for blind review, plus automated overlap metrics (ROUGE). If a quantized variant fails automated thresholds, flag for human review. The harness can be run as part of the load run pipeline.

[12:45] Laura Kim: On compliance, can you sign an NDA or a data processing addendum to allow us to share sanitized traces for replay?
[12:52] Maya Chen: Yes. We have a standard DPA and can sign an NDA; we'll attach legal contacts to the next steps.

[13:10] Jordan Li: Let's outline the immediate microbenchmark we're proposing:
- 6-hour run: includes 30m ramp, 4.5h steady-state, 30m high-burst windows every 45 minutes.
- Use Arcturus short+medium prompt mix (70/30 token distribution).
- Collect per-request CSV with kv_hit boolean and batch_size; collect GPU metrics every 10s.
- Run variants: hosted-FP16, hosted-INT8, dedicated-FP16, on-prem-FP16

[13:45] Evelyn Park: For on-prem the ops window needs to be during our maintenance period; can schedule overnight. We'll confirm.

[14:00] Jordan Li: We'll provide the k6 script and a containerized runner so you can execute with minimal setup. Also include an Ansible playbook to configure VPC peering stubs for the private test.

[14:22] [00:57:00] Samir Gupta: One objection to hosted — how do we ensure noise from multi-tenant kernels doesn't skew results? We require a dedicated or reserved lane for representative numbers.
[14:32] Maya Chen: For apples-to-apples, that is why Redwood Dedicated is recommended. For hosted runs we can allocate reserved capacity or coordinate quiet windows. We'll also annotate runs with load on the host to flag noisy neighbors.

[14:55] Rita Moreno: Any recommended thresholds for rolling decisions? Example: if INT8 reduces cost by 40% but increases p95 lat by 5% — what's acceptable?
[15:05] Noah Rivera: That depends on SLO. We recommend a matrix: if p95 increase <= 10% and human eval degradation <2% absolute on pass/fail, then tag as acceptable for non-critical paths. But customer must pick thresholds. We'll help run sensitivity analysis.

[15:30] Laura Kim: Security asks again — logs retention and encryption at rest for hosted: what's the default?
[15:37] Maya Chen: Default hosted retention is 30 days for trace data, archived logs can be extended. All logs are encrypted at rest with KMS; you can bring-your-own-key for enterprise plans.

[15:55] Jordan Li: Wrapping with concrete next steps: we'll upload the runbook and k6 script by Tue 8/25. Jordan will run the first KV microbenchmark using the sample prompt set and share results. Arcturus will provide anonymized prompt distribution and confirm windows for on-prem test. Legal contact exchange for DPA.

[16:20] Evelyn Park: Sounds good. Quick follow: can you include a short checklist for pre-flight — like expected docker images, rootfs, GPU drivers?
[16:28] Priya Shah: Yes — we'll add a 1-page preflight checklist.

[16:40] [summary and recap]
Maya Chen: Recap — deliverables from Redwood: runbook with normalization spreadsheet, k6 script and containerized runner, initial kv-cache microbenchmark CSVs, preflight checklist, legal contacts. From Arcturus: prompt distribution, maintenance window for on-prem, egress diagram.

[17:05] Rita Moreno: We'll aim to review the first microbenchmark results and meet again in two weeks.

[17:20] [closing]
Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. I'll follow up with calendar invites and attach the artifacts.
[17:30] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: Automated captions had a few mis-hearings ("kv cack"), timestamps approximated; speaker attribution was manually corrected in places.
